# Boston Building Energy Explorer: five-minute speaking outline

Total: 5:00. Timing includes the live filtering demonstration.

## 0:00–0:40 | Which buildings need a closer look?

Our decision problem is practical: among buildings with similar uses and sizes, which warrant an energy-efficiency investigation, and which records need a data-quality review first? The explorer serves planners, managers and community sustainability organizations. High energy intensity is a reason to ask questions. It does not demonstrate poor management. We use the 2025 disclosure release, but the energy-use year remains unconfirmed, so this presentation does not label it as 2025 consumption.

## 0:40–1:25 | Three populations, three purposes

The workbook required more than joining two sheets. The Summary says campus data was removed from the main sheet, but actual rows contradict that statement. We identified sections by headers and IDs and removed 544 repeated appearances. There are 5,487 unique building IDs, but only 5,034 are non-campus buildings. Aggregate energy uses those buildings plus one summary per campus, never campus members as well. Two campus references point to absent building records. The website discloses that mismatch.

## 1:25–2:15 | Live exploration with a fixed benchmark

I will demonstrate the live filters now. Choose Multifamily Housing, then a floor-area range from 25,000 to 50,000 square feet. The selected count, distribution, scatterplot and table update together. Select a ZIP if useful, then open a building. Notice that the peer median and sample size are fixed to the full eligible release, not recalculated from the visible subset. Reset returns the initial focus. Missing and flagged records remain searchable in the table even when they cannot enter the energy chart. The log scatterplot reports how many records it excludes.

## 2:15–3:10 | An investigation example: BERDO 100933

This is BERDO 100933, a multifamily building with a reported area of 3,996 square feet. Its calculated EUI is 525.0, compared with 73.7 for its 841 eligible peers. It exceeds the upper quartile and passes the project energy checks. At 50 percent gap closure, the benchmark scenario difference is 901,658 kBtu. This is arithmetic, not verified savings. A small reported area and unusual operations could help explain the result. The next step is to confirm the floor area, meter boundary and occupancy, then assess whether an engineering study is warranted.

## 3:10–4:10 | Findings support different next actions

Three observations support action. First, only 64.7 percent of non-campus records pass the energy-input rules; missing energy is the largest exclusion reason. That supports an effort to complete and reconcile submissions. Second, even the focus categories have broad EUI distributions. Their category medians are descriptive, not evidence that one use is inherently inefficient. Third, 666 buildings exceed their matched peer upper quartile. That supports collecting operating information for a focused investigation list. Separately, the negative electricity values at 102879 and 105219 require source review. Unrelated water and emissions flags do not automatically invalidate an energy comparison.

## 4:10–5:00 | A decision aid with explicit limits

This release does not establish trends or the effect of BERDO policy. Correlation cannot identify the causal effect of equipment or energy measures. We lack sufficient hours, occupancy, age, equipment performance, retrofit cost and energy-price information. Estimated emissions also do not determine final compliance. The contribution is narrower and useful: an inspectable way to separate questions about energy from questions about data, while keeping the reference population and formulas consistent. All analysis downloads, the methodology note and reflection are linked on the Data and Methods page. A real audit and corrected source data should guide any investment decision.

Sources: https://data.boston.gov/dataset/building-emissions-reduction-and-disclosure-ordinance/resource/911db0b1-437f-43ba-86bb-860cc1cd9319 and https://www.boston.gov/departments/environment/berdo
